title: Metric definition matters here more than usual
finding: This dataset totals 2.28T across 95,893 awards, but that figure is the sum of each award's *current total contract value* -- not dollars obligated during this specific window. A single large IDV or production contract (e.g. an F-35 Lot buy) shows its full multi-year ceiling the moment any action touches it, so awards active in a given year can sum to far more than DoD's actual annual budget. This is why FY2026 (7 months, partial) shows more value than any full prior year -- large production-lot contracts happened to get modified in that window, not a real spending spike. Treat this as 'value of the contract portfolio active in each period,' not 'dollars spent.'

title: Aircraft & Aviation Systems dominates by a wide margin
finding: Aircraft & Aviation Systems / Aircraft Manufacturing accounts for $633.8B, more than the next two categories combined. This tracks with the independently-built Spend Taxonomy analysis earlier in this project, which also found Aircraft & Aviation Systems as the largest DoD spend category.

title: Overall concentration is moderate; it's the categories that concentrate
finding: The department-wide supplier HHI is 704 (DOJ/FTC's own convention treats anything under 1500 as unconcentrated) -- unsurprising given 24,092 distinct suppliers. But the top 5 suppliers still capture 44.1% of total value, and several individual categories (see Categories & Opportunities tab) run well above 2500 HHI, meaning concentration is real, it's just masked at the whole-department level.

title: LOCKHEED MARTIN CORP is the largest single supplier by a wide margin
finding: $539.0B (23.6%) across 963 distinct awards -- driven heavily by F-35 Lightning II Low Rate Initial Production contracts, which individually run into the tens of billions. This is a scale observation, not a competition or performance finding.

title: Healthcare & Medical shows the clearest fragmentation signal
finding: $174,649,409,647 in this category is split across 228 suppliers; the largest (HUMANA GOVERNMENT BUSINESS INC) accounts for only 42% (HHI=2214). Fragmentation signal only -- not a specific vendor recommendation or savings estimate.

title: 6 pairs of same-supplier, same-category, similar-dollar awards flagged
finding: Close in time (within 120 days) and similar in size (within 30%) -- the 'two separate purchases instead of one consolidated buy' pattern. Not evidence of waste on its own; see the Standout tab for specifics.

title: 16% of awards are unclassified
finding: 15,464 of 95,893 awards didn't match this taxonomy's NAICS codes or keywords deterministically. Left as 'Other or Unclassified' rather than guessed, consistent with this project's rule that ambiguous records go to review, not a forced category.

title: Supplier resolution has one known gap: Lockheed Martin
finding: This dataset's supplier identity resolution uses recipient_parent_uei as its primary key, falling back to entity UEI or name -- a genuine improvement over facility-level UEI matching. But it still shows Lockheed Martin split across two entries in the Top Suppliers list ('LOCKHEED MARTIN CORP' and 'LOCKHEED MARTIN CORPORATION'), because some of its awards carry a registered parent UEI and others don't, resolving to different clusters even though it's the same company. A second pass that merged clusters by normalized company name was tried and reverted: it also merged genuinely unrelated small businesses that happen to share generic name fragments once corporate-suffix words are stripped (e.g. two different real companies both reducing to 'A A'), and it risked mishandling real acquisition history for at least one supplier. Between a disclosed split and an unreliable merge, this project keeps the split and discloses it here rather than risk silently combining unrelated companies.
